newsitem.title: CANADA: DE BEERS, BHP IN DIAMOND TALKS.
newsitem.headline: DE BEERS, BHP IN DIAMOND TALKS.

text.p: South Africa's De Beers Consolidated Mines Ltd said Wednesday that it has held preliminary talks with Australia's Broken Hill Proprietary Co Ltd on securing a deal to market diamonds from a BHP mine under development in Canada's Arctic region.

"We have had discussions at the highest level on the question of marketing. But we haven't really gotten down to talking to them in detail," De Beers director George Burne told the Canadian television program Business World.
"Obviously we look forward to doing that, and we hope they will advise us before too long," he said.
Burne spoke from Ottawa, where he said he gave a presentation to Canadian officials about De Beers.

Many analysts believe BHP will sell at least part of its output outside De Beers' London-based Central Selling Organisation which has controlled the world market in diamonds for more than 100 years through accords with producers.

BHP previously confirmed it was investigating independent marketing outside the CSO. BHP and joint venture partner Dia Met Minerals Ltd last week won final approval from the Canadian government to develop a C$900 million diamond mine at remote Lac de Gras in the Northwest Territories.
Burne said it would "not be the end of the world" if BHP failed to join the CSO. "Obviously we would like to work with them whatever they decide," he said.
The mine is slated to go into production in the second half of 1998. BHP said last week it expected to decide in about a year whether to market through De Beers.

The Lac de Gras mine is expected to produce three million to five million carats of diamonds a year, including many gems over its 25-year life. BHP has 51 percent of the project and Dia Met 29 percent. Two geologists who discovered the diamond deposit and are major Dia Met shareholders, control the rest.
Burne said Canadian government officials were interested in possible measures to assure security for the diamond mine, including legislation controlling who can hold rough diamonds.
